summary: Multilinear Galois Mode (MGM) is an authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) block cipher mode built on the Encrypt-then-MAC principle, defined for 64-bit and 128-bit block ciphers. It was standardized in Russia and is used with the GOST ciphers in protocols such as TLS 1.3 and IPsec. This informational document is a reference to enable review.

plainLanguage.summary: Some secret-code methods both scramble a message and check it was not tampered with. MGM is one such method, used in Russia, and this document writes it down so experts everywhere can inspect it.

subtitle: An AEAD encryption mode that encrypts data and authenticates it using the Galois field multilinear function.

tldr.problem: Secure communication needs to both scramble data (confidentiality) and prove it has not been modified (authentication). A single algorithm should do both efficiently, especially for Russian GOST block ciphers used in protocols like TLS 1.3 and IPsec.
tldr.mechanism: MGM (Multilinear Galois Mode) is an Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) mode that encrypts plaintext using counter mode and authenticates using a multilinear function based on the Galois field, producing both ciphertext and an authentication tag.
tldr.outcome: MGM standardized in Russia and is now specified in IETF RFC 9058 for use with any 64-bit or 128-bit block cipher, enabling international review and interoperability. The mode is parallelizable, supports online processing, and allows precomputation.

facts.label: Nonce requirement
facts.value: Must be unique for each message with the same key

facts.label: Cipher algorithms
facts.value: Kuznyechik (128-bit), Magma (64-bit), or any compatible cipher

today: RFC 9058 is Informational and published by the RFC Editor independently. MGM remains the standard AEAD mode for GOST ciphers in Russian standards and is used in TLS 1.3 and IPsec implementations for Russian cryptography.

sections.title: What MGM Does
sections.content:
Multilinear Galois Mode is a method for encrypting data and proving it has not been tampered with. It is an Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) mode, meaning it encrypts some data while also authenticating other data that is not encrypted (such as headers). MGM is based on the Encrypt-then-MAC (EtM) principle, where plaintext is encrypted first, then the encryption and associated data are authenticated together.

MGM was created in Russia and is used with GOST block ciphers (Kuznyechik for 128-bit blocks, Magma for 64-bit blocks) in real protocols including TLS 1.3 and IPsec. This RFC publishes MGM as an informational standard so cryptographers worldwide can review it and use it with any block cipher that has a 64-bit or 128-bit block size.

The mode is designed to be parallelizable (many encryption operations can run in parallel), inverse-free (the algorithm does not need to reverse the block cipher), and online (it can process messages as they arrive, not waiting for the full message length).
sections.plainLanguage: MGM is a recipe for turning a scrambling function into something that both scrambles data and proves nobody tampered with it. It was invented in Russia and is used in real security protocols.

sections.title: How MGM Works
sections.content:
MGM takes four inputs: an encryption key K, an initial counter nonce ICN (a unique value that must never be reused with the same key), associated authenticated data A (headers that are authenticated but not encrypted), and plaintext P to be encrypted and authenticated.

The encryption step encrypts plaintext using counter mode, where the nonce is incremented for each block to produce a stream of encryption pads. The plaintext is XORed with these pads to produce ciphertext.

The authentication step uses a multilinear function in the Galois field GF(2^n), where n is the block size. Separate counter sequences generate both encryption pads and authentication function values, minimizing overlap. The authentication sums XOR products of authentication values with plaintext and ciphertext blocks. The final authentication tag is produced by encrypting this sum.

The output is the ciphertext C and an authentication tag T. On the receiving end, the same process is repeated: if the computed tag matches the received tag, the data is authentic; if not, decryption fails.
sections.plainLanguage: MGM takes the plaintext and the key, then: (1) scrambles the data using math patterns that never repeat, (2) computes a checksum using special Galois field math to prove the data came from the owner, and (3) returns both the scrambled data and the checksum.

sections.title: Why MGM Is Secure
sections.content:
MGM's security rests on several design choices. Different counter functions (incr_r and incr_l) are used for encryption and authentication to minimize counter value overlap, preventing attackers from exploiting patterns. The multilinear function in the Galois field resists small subgroup attacks, and encrypting the function output prevents padding attacks. Encrypting the nonces (0^1 || ICN for encryption, 1^1 || ICN for authentication) minimizes the plaintext and ciphertext pairs known to attackers.

Critical security requirements: Every message encrypted with the same key must use a unique nonce. Reusing a nonce with the same key is catastrophic and eliminates all security. Never process empty plaintext and empty associated data at the same time; doing so makes the tag independent of the nonce and opens the mode to forgery attacks.

Security analysis shows that the confidentiality and integrity advantages are bounded by functions of the number of encryption queries and block sizes. The RFC specifies formulas for calculating how much data can be safely encrypted with a single key.
sections.plainLanguage: MGM is secure because it uses multiple independent counter sequences so attackers cannot find patterns, it uses math from the Galois field that is very hard to reverse, and it encrypts special nonces to keep attackers from collecting too many examples of plaintext and ciphertext.

sections.title: Using MGM in Protocols
sections.content:
When using MGM in a protocol like TLS or IPsec, the protocol specifies four parameters: the block cipher (e.g., Kuznyechik or any 128-bit cipher), the key length, the nonce length (usually 15 bytes for a 16-byte block, leaving 1 bit for mode selection), and the authentication tag length S (typically 128 bits for full authentication, but 32 to 64 bits may be acceptable depending on security requirements).

The protocol is responsible for ensuring that every (key, nonce) pair is unique. A common approach is to use part of the nonce as a counter incremented for each message. Associated authenticated data is typically network headers (source, destination, protocol type) that must be authenticated but not encrypted.

The RFC provides test vectors for Kuznyechik and Magma ciphers to help implementers verify their implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: When you use MGM in a real protocol, you pick a scrambling function (like Kuznyechik), decide how many bits for the checksum, and make sure you never use the same nonce twice with the same key.
